words.definition: open to more than one interpretation; ambiguous, often deliberately
words.nuance: Often implies deliberate vagueness to avoid commitment.
examples: The senator gave an equivocal answer about raising taxes.
The test results were equivocal, so the doctor ordered more scans.

words.definition: unclear, vague, or ill-defined
words.nuance: From nebula, a cloud of gas: hazy and shapeless.
examples: The company's plans for the merger remain nebulous.
He had only a nebulous idea of what the job involved.

words.definition: intended for or understood by only a small group with specialized knowledge
words.nuance: Obscure because it belongs to insiders.
examples: The lecture was full of esoteric references to medieval law.
Collecting antique fishing lures is an esoteric hobby.

words.definition: understood by few; mysterious or secret
words.nuance: Suggests secret or specialized knowledge.
examples: Tax law is full of arcane rules that few people understand.
The guild guarded its arcane techniques for centuries.

words.definition: difficult to understand; obscure
words.nuance: Hard because it is complex, not because it is secret.
examples: The philosopher's abstruse arguments lost most readers.
She explained the abstruse theory in plain language.

words.definition: little known; dealing with very profound or difficult subject matter
words.nuance: Scholarly obscurity.
examples: The professor's recondite research interested only a handful of specialists.
Crossword fans delight in recondite words.

words.definition: difficult to interpret or understand; mysterious
words.nuance: Often of people, smiles, or remarks.
examples: The Mona Lisa is famous for her enigmatic smile.
His enigmatic reply left us more confused than before.

words.definition: impossible to understand or interpret
words.nuance: Often of facial expressions that reveal nothing.
examples: The poker player kept an inscrutable expression.
Her motives remained inscrutable even to her closest friends.

words.definition: having a meaning that is mysterious or obscure
words.nuance: Often deliberately puzzling.
examples: She left a cryptic note on the kitchen table.
The poem's cryptic final line has puzzled readers for years.

words.definition: to make obscure, unclear, or hard to understand
words.nuance: Usually deliberate.
examples: The lawyer tried to obfuscate the facts with technical jargon.
Do not obfuscate a simple point with needless detail.

words.definition: to make clear; to explain
words.nuance: Shedding light on something puzzling.
examples: The professor drew a diagram to elucidate the process.
Further research may elucidate how the disease spreads.

words.definition: to analyze and develop an idea or text in detail
words.nuance: Typical of close readings of texts.
examples: The essay sets out to explicate a single difficult poem.
Scholars still explicate the clause line by line.

words.definition: superficially plausible but actually wrong
words.nuance: Looks true at first glance; that is the trap.
examples: The ad made the specious claim that the pill burned fat during sleep.
Her argument was specious, resting on a misleading statistic.

words.definition: not genuine or authentic; based on false reasoning
words.nuance: Fake, or falsely appearing to be true.
examples: The study found a spurious link between shoe size and intelligence.
Collectors were fooled by a spurious signature.

words.definition: based on a mistaken belief or unsound reasoning
words.nuance: Contains a logical fallacy.
examples: The conclusion rests on a fallacious assumption.
It is fallacious to argue that rare events never happen.

words.definition: of doubtful authenticity, though widely circulated as true
words.nuance: Typical of famous anecdotes and quotations.
examples: The story of the apple falling on Newton's head is probably apocryphal.
Many apocryphal quotes are attributed to Einstein.

words.definition: to confirm or give support to a statement, theory, or finding
words.nuance: Usually with additional, independent evidence.
examples: Two witnesses were able to corroborate her account.
New data corroborate the original hypothesis.

words.definition: to provide evidence to support or prove the truth of
words.nuance: Backing up a claim with evidence.
examples: The reporter could not substantiate the rumor.
You must substantiate any claim with data.

words.definition: to support or strengthen
words.nuance: A bolster is literally a long supporting pillow.
examples: The new evidence will bolster the prosecution's case.
Good reviews helped bolster the author's confidence.

words.definition: to increase the strength of or justify; to support
words.nuance: From the architectural support built against a wall.
examples: She cited three studies to buttress her argument.
Engineers had to buttress the old wall with steel beams.

words.definition: to strengthen, especially against attack
words.nuance: Also used for adding nutrients to food.
examples: The town built walls to fortify its defenses.
A good breakfast will fortify you for the long hike.

words.definition: having or showing great knowledge or learning
words.nuance: Knowledge gained from study and reading.
examples: The erudite historian could quote sources in five languages.
Her erudite essay impressed even the specialists.

words.definition: having keen discernment and good judgment; wise
words.nuance: Wisdom that comes from experience.
examples: The sagacious investor sold just before the crash.
Villagers sought the sagacious elder's advice.

words.definition: able to assess situations or people accurately and use this to one's advantage
words.nuance: Sharp, practical intelligence.
examples: An astute observer would have noticed the error.
Her astute questions exposed the plan's weaknesses.

words.definition: having a ready insight into and understanding of things
words.nuance: Seeing clearly what others miss.
examples: The perspicacious critic saw the film's flaws at once.
A perspicacious teacher notices when a student is struggling.

words.definition: abundant in supply or quantity
words.nuance: Often of notes, food, or rain.
examples: She took copious notes during the lecture.
The storm brought copious rain to the valley.

words.definition: exuberantly plentiful; abundant
words.nuance: Often of things that pour out: apologies, sweat, flowers.
examples: He offered profuse apologies for the delay.
The garden was a profuse tangle of roses.

words.definition: an excessive amount; an overabundance
words.nuance: Strictly means too much, though often used to mean simply 'a lot'.
examples: The report contained a plethora of charts but little analysis.
Shoppers face a plethora of nearly identical phones.

words.definition: an excessive amount of something
words.nuance: Often implies discomfort from having too much.
examples: A surfeit of sugar can ruin a dessert.
The market suffered from a surfeit of cheap imports.

words.definition: a scarcity or lack of something
words.nuance: Common in GRE passages: 'a dearth of evidence'.
examples: The region suffers from a dearth of clean water.
There is no dearth of opinions on the subject.

words.definition: the presence of something in only small or insufficient quantities
words.nuance: Formal; stresses insufficiency.
examples: The paucity of evidence made a conviction unlikely.
Critics noted the paucity of women in the cast.

words.definition: causing harm or damage
words.nuance: Often of gradual harm to health or the environment.
examples: Smoking has deleterious effects on almost every organ.
Lack of sleep can be deleterious to memory.

words.definition: having a harmful effect, especially in a gradual or subtle way
words.nuance: Harm that spreads quietly.
examples: The pernicious rumor slowly destroyed trust in the office.
Mold can cause pernicious damage behind walls.

words.definition: harmful, poisonous, or very unpleasant
words.nuance: Often of gases or fumes.
examples: The factory released noxious fumes into the air.
His noxious comments poisoned the meeting.

words.definition: not harmful or offensive
words.nuance: Can also mean bland and unremarkable.
examples: The question seemed innocuous, but it upset her.
Most spiders are innocuous to humans.

words.definition: not harmful; also, gentle and kindly
words.nuance: In medicine, a benign tumor is not cancerous.
examples: The doctor confirmed that the growth was benign.
A benign climate made the island popular with retirees.

words.definition: suggesting a positive and successful future
words.nuance: Good signs at the start of something.
examples: The team got off to an auspicious start with three straight wins.
It was an auspicious day for a wedding.

words.definition: giving or indicating a good chance of success; favorable
words.nuance: Favorable conditions or timing.
examples: The calm weather was propitious for sailing.
She waited for a propitious moment to ask for a raise.

words.definition: still in existence; surviving
words.nuance: Usually of documents, species, or works from the past.
examples: Only two copies of the manuscript are extant.
It is the oldest extant building in the city.

words.definition: dealing with things sensibly and realistically
words.nuance: Practical results over theory or ideals.
examples: The mayor took a pragmatic approach to the budget crisis.
Rather than argue about theory, she offered a pragmatic solution.

words.definition: exceedingly idealistic; unrealistic and impractical
words.nuance: From Don Quixote, who attacked windmills he took for giants.
examples: His quixotic plan to end world hunger in a year was doomed.
Some called her campaign quixotic, but she won.

words.definition: producing much fruit, offspring, or work
words.nuance: Very often of writers, artists, and inventors.
examples: The prolific author published three novels a year.
Rabbits are famously prolific breeders.

words.definition: producing or capable of producing abundant offspring or new growth; fertile
words.nuance: Used for land, animals, and imaginations.
examples: The fecund river valley fed the whole region.
She had a fecund imagination that produced endless stories.

words.definition: optimistic or positive, especially in a difficult situation
words.nuance: An old meaning is 'blood-red'; on the GRE it means hopeful.
examples: Despite the losses, the coach remained sanguine about the season.
Economists are less sanguine about next year's growth.

words.definition: cheerful and optimistic; also, able to float
words.nuance: Also used for markets that stay strong.
examples: The team was in a buoyant mood after the victory.
The buoyant sales figures lifted the company's stock.

words.definition: unwilling or unable to believe something
words.nuance: Describes the person who doubts, not the thing doubted.
examples: She gave an incredulous laugh when she heard the price.
The incredulous fans watched the underdog win.

words.definition: having or showing too great a readiness to believe things
words.nuance: Too trusting; easily fooled.
examples: The credulous investors poured money into an obvious scam.
Only a credulous reader would believe that headline.

words.definition: innocent and unsuspecting; artless
words.nuance: Not the same as ingenious (clever); disingenuous is its opposite.
examples: Her ingenuous questions charmed the older guests.
It would be ingenuous to assume the deal has no catch.

words.definition: truthful and straightforward; frank
words.nuance: Honest even when the truth is uncomfortable.
examples: The CEO gave a candid account of the company's mistakes.
I appreciate your candid feedback.

words.definition: direct and outspoken; straightforward
words.nuance: Says plainly what one thinks.
examples: She was forthright about her reasons for leaving.
A forthright reply is better than an evasive one.

words.definition: kept secret or done secretively, especially because illicit
words.nuance: Organized secrecy: meetings, operations, affairs.
examples: The rebels held clandestine meetings in a basement.
Their clandestine romance lasted for years.

words.definition: kept secret, especially because it would not be approved of
words.nuance: Often of quick, sneaky actions.
examples: He took a surreptitious glance at his phone during the meeting.
The surreptitious recording was later used in court.

words.definition: attempting to avoid notice, typically because of guilt
words.nuance: Suggests nervous guilt.
examples: The thief cast a furtive look over his shoulder.
Their furtive whispers stopped when the teacher walked in.

words.definition: present, appearing, or found everywhere
words.nuance: Often slightly exaggerated: seemingly everywhere.
examples: Smartphones have become ubiquitous in modern life.
The ubiquitous coffee chain has a store on every corner.

words.definition: spreading widely throughout an area or group
words.nuance: Often of something unwelcome: a pervasive smell or fear.
examples: A pervasive sense of anxiety filled the city.
Corruption was pervasive in the old regime.
